Where is Virginia Beach, and how is the city organized?

Virginia Beach is the most populous city in Virginia, sitting on the Atlantic Ocean at the mouth of the Chesapeake Bay in the southeastern corner of the state. It is about 19 miles east of Norfolk and 107 miles southeast of Richmond.

The city has almost 245 square miles of land and about 253 square miles of water, with an average elevation near 12 feet. A major portion drains to the Chesapeake Bay through the Lynnhaven River and its tributaries.

An urban growth boundary called the Green Line divides the developed north from the rural south. The city has begun to run short of clear land north of that line, which keeps attention on existing homes and redevelopment.

How did Virginia Beach become one city?

The modern city was created in 1963, when the 253-square-mile Princess Anne County merged with the 2-square-mile resort city of Virginia Beach. The merged city was divided into seven boroughs: Bayside, Blackwater, Kempsville, Lynnhaven, Princess Anne, Pungo and Virginia Beach.

Because of that merger, a Virginia Beach address can mean a beachfront block, a suburban subdivision or a farm. The city includes communities such as Sandbridge, Kempsville, Thalia, Great Neck Point, Bayside, Oceana, Pungo and Green Run, each with its own feel.

When you describe your house to a buyer, name the community, since a ten-minute drive can change the buyer pool.

What does flooding mean for a Virginia Beach house?

Flooding is the main environmental issue for many Virginia Beach homes, given the low elevation and the amount of surrounding water. Heavy rain from Hurricane Matthew flooded more than 2,000 homes and left some neighborhoods under standing water for days.

After that storm the city turned down several proposed floodplain developments, which the developers challenged in court without success. The episode shows how seriously the city treats flood risk.

  • Ask your insurer whether your parcel needs flood coverage and what the premium is.
  • Gather any elevation certificates, repair records and insurance claims, since buyers ask for them.
  • Tell a cash buyer about past water in the house. A direct buyer can price in the damage instead of the sale falling apart at inspection.

Who are the largest employers in Virginia Beach?

Military bases, tourism and corporate headquarters make up most of the economy. NAS Oceana is the largest employer in the city, and the Joint Expeditionary Base East at Cape Henry, Training Support Center Hampton Roads and Naval Amphibious Base Little Creek are also in or beside the city.

Other employers include the Christian Broadcasting Network, the U.S. headquarters of Stihl, and GEICO. The city has about 172 farms, mostly south of the Green Line.

Owners tied to the bases sometimes need to sell on a set date, and that is when closing certainty matters most.

How do you get around Virginia Beach?

Norfolk International Airport serves the city and sits along the city line with Norfolk. Amtrak service runs through the Norfolk and Newport News stations with connecting buses, and Hampton Roads Transit buses serve Atlantic Avenue.

The Virginia Breeze intercity bus line added a Virginia Beach stop at the Convention Center on April 20, 2026. The route, called the Tidewater Current, connects to Norfolk, Newport News, Williamsburg, Richmond, Charlottesville and Staunton.

A Greyhound station is on Laskin Road, about a mile west of the oceanfront. Parking and commute time are standard buyer questions.

What is Virginia Beach known for, and does it affect a sale?

Virginia Beach is a resort city with a long oceanfront. Guinness lists it as having the longest pleasure beach in the world, and Cape Henry was the site of the first landing of the English colonists in 1607 before they settled Jamestown.

Town Center opened in 2003 and the Convention Center in 2005, both built with public and private money and tax increment financing. The Alan B. Shepard Civic Center, called the Dome, reopened in 2025.

Tourism supports hotels, restaurants and short-term rentals near the oceanfront. If your house is near the resort area, ask the city's planning office about short-term rental rules before you advertise it that way, because we did not confirm those rules from an official page.

When are Virginia Beach real estate taxes due?

Real estate taxes in Virginia Beach are billed by the City Treasurer in two installments, due December 5 and June 5. If a date falls on a weekend or city holiday, the deadline moves to the next business day.

  • The tax year is the city's fiscal year, July 1 through June 30, and taxes are paid in arrears.
  • For proration at a sale, taxes are calculated daily using the full annual tax for that fiscal year.
  • A late payment carries a 10% penalty or $10, whichever is greater, plus interest at 9.6% a year, according to the Treasurer.
  • If a mortgage company pays through escrow, the bill goes to the lender, so tell the Treasurer when the loan ends.

Ownership records in the Real Estate Assessor's Office are updated from deeds recorded with the Clerk of the Circuit Court. Details are on the Virginia Beach Treasurer's real estate page.

What other taxes apply when you sell in Virginia Beach?

Virginia's deed taxes apply on top of property taxes. The state recordation tax is 25 cents per $100 under section 58.1-801, and the seller's grantor tax is 50 cents per $500 under section 58.1-802.

The deed must state the price on its first page before it is recorded. The Treasurer says delinquent taxes are collected before a refund is issued, so clear any old balance before closing.

Do inherited or estate sales follow special rules in Virginia Beach?

The Residential Property Disclosure Act excludes transfers by a fiduciary administering an estate, guardianship, conservatorship or trust. The exclusions are listed in section 55.1-702.

The same section excludes transfers after foreclosure and transfers between spouses or to lineal relatives. Ask an estate attorney which category covers your sale.

Is a cash sale a good fit for a Virginia Beach seller?

It can be, especially when flood damage, deferred repairs, tenants or a military move make a listing hard. A cash buyer purchases without a lender, so the sale does not hinge on a buyer's mortgage approval.

It is worth comparing against a listing. Ask for a written offer and calculate what you keep after taxes, repairs and holding costs.

Yes. Many buyers shy away from flood damage, but a direct cash buyer can price the repairs in and buy as is. Gather any insurance claims and repair records first.

What kind of city is Chesapeake, and how big is it?

Chesapeake is an independent city in the Hampton Roads area of southeastern Virginia, and by land area it is the second largest city in the state. It covers about 351 square miles, of which roughly 338 are land, so a house here can sit in a dense neighborhood near Norfolk or on a rural road close to the North Carolina line.

The Census Bureau counted 249,422 residents in 2020 and estimates 255,332 for 2025, which makes Chesapeake the second most populous city in Virginia. Much of the land is protected farmland, forest and wetland, including part of the Great Dismal Swamp National Wildlife Refuge. The Atlantic Intracoastal Waterway and the Elizabeth River run through the developed areas.

For a seller, the size matters. A buyer who knows Great Bridge may know nothing about Deep Creek or Western Branch, and the same repair problem can mean something different in each.

How did Chesapeake become a city?

Chesapeake was created in 1963, when the independent city of South Norfolk and the remaining part of Norfolk County voted to consolidate and took a new name. Norfolk County itself dated to 1691, and most of its original territory had already been annexed by neighboring cities.

The old county produced a patchwork of communities rather than one town center. Wikipedia lists six boroughs: South Norfolk, Butts Road, Deep Creek, Pleasant Grove, Western Branch and Washington. Great Bridge, where the Battle of Great Bridge was fought on December 9, 1775, is another community name sellers and buyers use every day.

Until the late 1980s much of the city was suburban or rural and served as a bedroom community for Norfolk and Virginia Beach. Growth through the 1990s brought its own employers and strained roads, schools and water supply. Houses built in different decades therefore have quite different systems, lot sizes and repair histories.

The largest employers in Chesapeake are the public school system and the city government. The city's 2025 annual financial report, as summarized on Wikipedia, ranks the top ten like this:

What does Chesapeake's climate and water mean for a house?

Chesapeake has a humid subtropical climate with hot, humid summers and mild to cool winters. Average daily highs run about 88 degrees in July and about 50 in January, and yearly precipitation averages roughly 48 inches, according to the climate table on Wikipedia drawn from 1980 to 2010 data.

The elevation is only about 16 feet, and the city sits among tidal rivers, canals and swamp. A house here can have drainage problems, a damp crawl space or a site that floods in heavy rain. Buyers and appraisers look at these points closely, and they are common reasons a listed house sits.

  • Check the crawl space for standing water, rot in the floor framing and failed vapor barriers.
  • Look at gutters, grading and any sump or French drain that has been added.
  • Ask the city or your insurer about the flood zone before you set a price, since flood status affects what buyers can insure.
  • Note roof age, because humid summers and storm winds shorten shingle life.

Water supply has its own history here. Chesapeake draws most of its drinking water from the Northwest River and treats it with reverse osmosis because the river is salty at times, and the region also receives water from Lake Gaston through a 76-mile pipeline.

How do roads, bridges and transit shape selling a house in Chesapeake?

Commute access is one of the first things buyers ask about, and Chesapeake has a lot of it. Interstate 64 forms part of the Hampton Roads Beltway through the city, I-464 links to downtown Norfolk and Portsmouth, and I-664 runs toward Newport News. U.S. 13, 17, 58 and 460 also serve the city, along with State Route 168, which includes the Chesapeake Expressway toll road.

The city maintains 90 bridges and overpasses, including five drawbridges that open an estimated 30,000 times a year for boats. Anyone who has waited at a bridge opening knows it can change how a particular address feels at rush hour. Hampton Roads Transit buses serve the city, and the nearest commercial airport is Norfolk International.

A listing agent will usually point to the route a buyer takes to the shipyards, the bases or downtown Norfolk. If your house is far from the interstate, a quick cash sale avoids waiting for a commuter to find it.

The city also lists May 15 as the application deadline for real estate tax relief for disabled owners and seniors, and it runs separate pages for disabled veteran benefits and surviving spouse exemptions.

Look up the current tax rate on the city's Local Tax Rates page rather than relying on an old bill, since the council sets it each year.

Who pays taxes and transfer costs when a Chesapeake house sells?

Under Virginia law, unpaid real estate taxes are a lien that comes ahead of other liens, and the lien continues until the taxing authority is actually paid. The state statute says the seller's liability for taxes is prorated by contract, so your sales contract decides who covers which days.

The state also charges a grantor tax of 50 cents for each $500 of the sale price, paid by the seller unless the two sides agree otherwise. The deed must show the price on its first page, and the clerk of court collects the tax when the deed is recorded. A few points to settle early:

  • Ask the Treasurer for a payoff figure on any unpaid installment before closing.
  • Confirm in writing who pays the grantor tax and recording costs.
  • Have the title company check for liens, judgments and unpaid utility charges.
  • If the house is part of an estate, confirm who has authority to sign the deed.

What do sellers in Chesapeake usually face?

Sellers here tend to run into the same few problems, and they are usually about the house rather than the market. Water damage from low ground, deferred repairs on older South Norfolk and Deep Creek homes, and tenant-occupied properties are the most common.

  • Inherited houses that nobody lives in, with taxes and insurance still due.
  • Properties with rot, mold or moisture problems that rule out standard financing.
  • Owners relocating for a military or civilian transfer on a short timeline.
  • Rental houses with a tenant or a lapsed lease.

A cash buyer purchases the house in its current condition, so you do not have to schedule repairs, staging or showings. We can buy directly or bring a vetted cash buyer, and we explain which route applies when we make an offer. You can compare that against listing and decide.

Chesapeake lists four installments: September 30, December 31, March 31 and June 5. Confirm the amount with the Treasurer's office before closing, because any unpaid balance is paid from the sale proceeds.

Does Virginia charge a tax when I sell a house?

Yes, there is a grantor tax of 50 cents per $500 of the sale price, and the seller normally pays it unless the contract says otherwise. Your title company will show the exact amount on the settlement statement.

Yes. A cash buyer can purchase a house with moisture problems or a crawl space in poor shape, and the offer reflects the repairs. A flood zone affects insurance for a financed buyer more than it affects a cash buyer.

Call the City Real Estate Assessor at 757-382-6235. The city says it assesses at 100 percent of fair market value, and the assessor can explain how your property was valued.

Do I need to be in Chesapeake to sell my house?

No. Owners who live elsewhere, including military families who have moved, can handle the sale remotely with signed documents and a local title company.

How is Richmond, Virginia, divided, and what does that mean for a house sale?

Richmond is usually described in four parts: the North Side, Southside, East End and West End. Each has its own housing mix, from Victorian townhouses to mid-century ranches, so the story of a Richmond house depends heavily on which side of the James River it is on.

The city is Virginia's capital and its fourth most populous city. The Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 237,257 residents, up from 226,610 in the 2020 census. Richmond has been an independent city since 1871, so there is no county layer between you and city hall.

Where do Richmond's neighborhoods sit?

Richmond's original street grid dates to 1737 and covered the area between today's Broad, 17th and 25th streets and the river. Modern downtown sits slightly west of that, on the slopes of Shockoe Hill.

  • East End: includes Church Hill, home to St. John's Church, along with Fulton, Union Hill and Fairmount.
  • The Fan and Museum District: the area between the Boulevard, Main Street and Broad Street, with Monument Avenue and many Victorian buildings, next to the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts.
  • Carytown: the commercial strip along Cary Street between Interstate 195 and the Boulevard.
  • North Side: many listed historic districts, including Ginter Park, Barton Heights, Highland Park and Chestnut Hill-Plateau, developed after the streetcar arrived.
  • West End: suburban in feel, with Windsor Farms among its best-known sections.
  • Southside: Westover Hills, Forest Hill, Woodland Heights, Stratford Hills and Old Town Manchester, among others.

The Southside has a different history from the rest of the city. Richmond absorbed the former city of Manchester in 1910, and on January 1, 1970 the city grew south by 27 square miles and gained 47,000 residents, after Chesterfield County lost a court fight against the annexation.

The Richmond metro area includes several Fortune 500 companies: Performance Food Group, Altria, CarMax, Dominion Energy, Markel, Owens and Minor, Genworth Financial and ARKO Corp. Capital One also has significant offices in the city.

Health and research add to this mix. Virginia Commonwealth University and its Medical College of Virginia campus anchor the Virginia BioTechnology Research Park, which opened in 1995 and has more than 575,000 square feet of lab and office space.

A multimillion-dollar flood wall was completed in 1995 to protect the low-lying parts of the city from the rising river. Shockoe Bottom, the low area between Shockoe Hill and Church Hill, is described as historically significant and low-lying.

Richmond has a humid subtropical climate with hot, humid summers and moderately cold winters. Snow averages 10.5 inches a season, and snow usually stays on the ground only a day or two.

There are exceptions. Snow stayed 16 days in early 2010 and 17 days in 2026, from January 25 to February 10. Ice storms are not unusual, though they are seldom severe enough to cause widespread damage, and tornadoes are infrequent.

For a seller, older roofs, gutters and pipes in unheated vacant houses are the usual pressure points. A vacant house in a cold snap can turn a small plumbing issue into a large repair bill.

Richmond is home to the Supreme Court of Virginia, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit, one of the four divisions of the Eastern District of Virginia and one of the four divisions of its Bankruptcy Court.

Richmond's downtown has long been a hub: boats at the Great Turning Basin, rail with one of only two triple rail crossings in North America, and two intersecting major interstates. Interstates 95, 64 and 195 all touch the city's neighborhoods.

The distance to jobs matters in this area. Richmond is about 21 miles north of Petersburg and part of the larger Richmond-Petersburg metro area, which includes surrounding counties such as Chesterfield, Henrico and Hanover.

Where is Norfolk, Virginia, and how big is it?

Norfolk is an independent city in the southeastern corner of Virginia, where the Elizabeth River meets the Chesapeake Bay. It is not part of any county, so the city handles its own assessments, tax billing and zoning.

The city covers 96.41 square miles, but only 53.28 of those are land. The other 43.13 square miles are water, and the average elevation is about 6.9 feet. The 2020 census counted 238,005 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 231,013.

How did Norfolk grow into the city it is today?

Norfolk began as a colonial seaport in the late 1600s and received a royal borough charter in 1736. It was incorporated as a city in 1845.

The Navy shaped the modern city. The 1907 Jamestown Exposition at Sewell's Point led to a naval air station in 1917, which became Naval Station Norfolk, the largest naval base in the world.

Highway building changed where people lived. The Downtown Tunnel opened in 1952, the Hampton Roads Bridge-Tunnel in 1957, the Midtown Tunnel in 1962 and the Virginia Beach-Norfolk Expressway in 1967. Those links helped suburbs form and pulled residents out of older neighborhoods.

Norfolk has a humid subtropical climate, and flooding is the main building concern. The city is low, mostly surrounded by water and slowly subsiding, and some areas already flood at high tide.

The City of Norfolk publishes flood zone rules on its Flood Zones page. The Flood Insurance Rate Map from FEMA sets the zones, and the city enforces them through Article 3.9.7 of its zoning ordinance and the Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code. The city lists these zones:

The Virginia Port Authority is headquartered in the city and operates Norfolk International Terminals. Maersk Line, Limited and several other shipping firms have North American offices here. Sentara Health is also headquartered in Norfolk.

For sellers, this can mean timing set by orders. A military household that gets new orders may need to close in a few weeks, and a landlord with a tenant on a short lease may want out before the next rotation. Cash sales fit those schedules because there is no loan approval to wait on.

  • Second quarter: due December 5.
  • Third quarter: due March 31.
  • Fourth quarter: due June 5.

The same page notes that the Treasurer collects nuisance abatement liens sent over by Neighborhood Quality, with 30 days to pay. If a Norfolk house has had weeds, trash or structure problems cleaned up by the city, ask the Treasurer for a payoff before you list or sign a contract.

What do Norfolk sellers usually face?

Most Norfolk sellers deal with a handful of repeat problems, and the location explains many of them.

  • Water damage in crawl spaces, basements and first floors on low lots.
  • Older houses with outdated wiring, plumbing or roofs.
  • Inherited houses with several heirs and no clear next step.

Use the city's Forerunner site, linked from the Flood Zones page. It shows the zone, flood data and any elevation certificates on file for a property.

Can I sell a Norfolk house with unpaid city liens?

Yes, but the liens are normally paid from the sale proceeds at closing. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff on any nuisance abatement charge and the settlement agent for the rest.

Who pays the Virginia grantor tax on a Norfolk sale?

The seller pays unless the contract says the buyer will cover some or all of it. The rate is 50 cents for each $500 of value under Virginia Code 58.1-802.

Newport News was a rural area and fishing village until the railroad arrived. In 1881 Collis P. Huntington's Peninsula Extension of the Chesapeake and Ohio Railway opened a way to bring coal to port, and a large shipyard followed within a few years. The city was incorporated in 1896.

Where is Alexandria, VA, and how is the city laid out?

Alexandria is an independent city on the west bank of the Potomac River, directly across from Washington, D.C. and Prince George's County, Maryland. It covers about 15.5 square miles, with Arlington County to the north and northwest and Fairfax County to the south.

The city was founded in 1749, became a town in 1779 and was re-chartered as a city in 1852. It split from Alexandria County in 1870. Two annexations, one in 1930 and one in 1952, each roughly doubled the land area, which is why the western half of the city looks and feels so different from Old Town.

That patchwork shows up in street numbering. In Old Town, house numbers run north and south from King Street and west from the river. In Del Ray and St. Elmo they run east and west from Commonwealth Avenue. Out west, numbers run north and south from Duke Street. If you are describing your house to a buyer, an appraiser or a title company, the neighborhood name matters as much as the street address.

Many mailing addresses with an Alexandria return line sit in Fairfax County, not inside the city. Before you assume the rules in this guide apply to you, confirm that your parcel is within city limits.

What are the main neighborhoods a seller should know about?

What does the local economy mean for house sellers in Alexandria?

Alexandria's housing demand follows federal and professional jobs, and most of the people who work in the city live somewhere else. About 13 percent of people who work in Alexandria also live there, while about 87 percent commute in. Roughly 61,000 residents commute out, with about 35 percent heading to Washington, D.C.

The largest public employers listed by the city are the Department of Defense at Mark Center with about 8,000 employees and the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office with about 6,000. The City of Alexandria itself employs about 2,600, Alexandria City Public Schools about 2,500, and Inova Health System leads the private list at about 2,500. Tourism is also large: visitor revenue passed $1 billion in 2024 for the first time.

For a seller, that mix has two effects. Federal relocations and contract changes can push owners to sell on short notice. And because so many buyers commute, houses close to a Metro station or the I-395 corridor usually draw different buyers than houses on the quieter western streets.

Metro stations opened in 1983 at King Street, Braddock Road and Eisenhower Avenue, in 1991 at Van Dorn Street and in May 2023 at Potomac Yard. The city bus system, DASH, began in 1984.

Does Alexandria have flood risk that affects a sale?

Yes, parts of Alexandria flood, and the city says about 20 percent of its area was mapped in a FEMA floodplain as of 2011. Heavy storms can also flood places outside the mapped zones.

The city's own storm sewer study found 83 problem areas across eight watersheds. Hooff's Run and Four Mile Run each had 23 of them. The sewers are built to a 10-year storm standard, and the city notes that the July 23, 2020 storm was about 30 times more intense than that. Hooff's Run carries water from parts of Northridge, Del Ray and Rosemont, so owners in those areas hear about drainage often.

Alexandria participates in the National Flood Insurance Program's Community Rating System as a Class 6 community, which can mean up to a 20 percent discount on flood insurance premiums. The city also runs a flood mitigation grant program and offers help with sewer backflow prevention. Read the details on the city's flooding and drainage page.

Virginia's residential property disclosure form tells buyers that the owner makes no statement about whether a house is in a special flood hazard area and points them to FEMA maps and the state's flood risk site. Even so, a basement that took water in a storm is something buyers ask about, and a written answer protects you.

Do historic district rules affect selling or fixing a house in Alexandria?

They can, because the city's Board of Architectural Review controls exterior changes in two local historic districts and on designated buildings that are 100 years old or older. The Old and Historic Alexandria District is the third historic district created in the country.

The board approves a Certificate of Appropriateness for new construction and for exterior changes to structures visible from a public way. It must also approve a Permit to Demolish for removing more than 25 square feet of material from a structure, whether or not it can be seen from the street. The Parker Gray District is the second local district.

This matters in a sale in two ways. A buyer who plans a renovation will price in the review time. And if you want to fix a roof, replace windows or tear out a porch before listing, you may need approval first. The city's preservation staff can be reached at preservation@alexandriava.gov or 703.746.3833, and the preservation page has a tool for checking whether a property is under review. The city has also been discussing zoning text changes that touch the two districts and the 100-year-old building list, so confirm current rules with staff.

A house that needs work and sits in a district is a common reason sellers choose an as-is cash sale, because the buyer takes on the approval process.

What are Alexandria's short-term rental rules if my house was an Airbnb?

Any Alexandria property rented for fewer than 30 consecutive days for more than 10 days in a calendar year needs a Short-Term Residential Rental Permit from the Department of Planning and Zoning. The annual permit fee is $350 for an owner-unoccupied rental and $100 for an owner-occupied one. The city said it would process permits in batches through summer 2026. Operators must also give guests a Good Neighbor Guide at least 24 hours before check-in and install required safety equipment.

If you are selling a house that has been used this way, gather the permit paperwork or application records before you list. A buyer will want to know whether the permit transfers or whether a new owner must start over, and the city is the only source for that answer. Contact the department through the short-term rental page.

What does a seller owe when the deed is recorded in Alexandria?

Virginia puts a state-and-local grantor's tax on the seller at 50 cents for each $500 of the sale price, unless the buyer agrees in the contract to pay some or all of it. That amount is split evenly between the state and the locality, and the clerk of the circuit court will not record the deed until it is paid.

Two more state rules matter at closing. First, unpaid real estate taxes are a lien that comes ahead of every other lien, so the settlement agent must pay them from your proceeds. The seller's share of the current year's tax is normally prorated in the contract. Second, you must give the buyer the Real Estate Board's residential property disclosure statement, which tells the buyer you make no promises about things like historic district rules, flood hazard areas, wastewater systems and radon, and urges the buyer to check for themselves.

We do not set the recording charges. Your settlement agent will quote them, and the statute is posted at Virginia Code 58.1-802.

How much is the Alexandria short-term rental permit?

Does Alexandria flood?

The seller pays it by default, at 50 cents per $500 of the sale price, but the contract can shift some or all of it to the buyer. Check your purchase agreement and ask the settlement agent for the exact figure.

Can I sell an Alexandria house as-is if it needs major repairs?

Yes. Virginia's disclosure form is built around the idea that the buyer inspects the house, and an as-is sale to a cash buyer is common for houses that need work. You still give the buyer the Real Estate Board's disclosure statement.

Fort Monroe, at Old Point Comfort, became a place of refuge for people escaping slavery during the Civil War. The Army decommissioned the base on September 15, 2011, and it was named a National Monument on November 1 of that year.   • Fox Hill
  • Hampton Woods
  • Northampton
  • Newmarket

  • Victoria Boulevard Historic District
  • Wythe, including the Olde Wythe Historic District

Houses in the historic districts can be decades or more than a century old. Older framing, original wiring and aging plumbing are common reasons a Hampton owner prefers to sell as-is instead of paying for repairs first.

Who employs people in Hampton, and does that affect a sale?

Hampton's economy leans heavily on federal aviation and research work. Langley Air Force Base is the home of the 633rd Air Base Wing and the 1st and 192nd Fighter Wings, and NASA's Langley Research Center is also in the city. Hampton University and Virginia Peninsula Community College add education jobs.

Military and federal households move on a schedule set by orders, not by the housing calendar. An owner who is transferred out of the Hampton Roads area may need to close in weeks. A sale that depends on a buyer's mortgage approval, appraisal and inspection can slip past that date.

Hampton also borders Newport News and Poquoson, and Williamsburg and Yorktown are nearby. Many residents work in a different city from the one they live in, so a house in Hampton is often judged by its commute as much as by its block.

How do roads and bridge-tunnels affect where a Hampton house sits?

Water crossings define travel here. Interstate 64 uses the Hampton Roads Bridge-Tunnel near downtown Hampton, and Interstate 664 uses the Monitor-Merrimac Memorial Bridge-Tunnel a few miles away. The two interstates converge near the Hampton Coliseum.

Other main routes are U.S. 17, U.S. 60 and U.S. 258, plus State Routes 134 and 143. Hampton Roads Transit runs public transportation, and the Hampton Transit Center is close to downtown.

Homes close to an interstate ramp or tunnel approach tend to have shorter commutes and more road noise. Sellers should expect a buyer to ask about both.

What does the weather do to a house in Hampton?

Hampton has a humid subtropical climate with hot, humid summers and mild winters. The mean annual temperature is 60.2 degrees Fahrenheit, with about 47 inches of rain and about 6 inches of snow in an average year. The wettest month on average is August.

Moisture is the practical issue. With rainfall that high and so much surrounding water, crawl spaces, basements, roofs and drainage are the areas inspectors look at first. The temperature record runs from 105.1 degrees in August 1980 to minus 2.7 degrees in January 1985, so heating and cooling systems both get used hard.

How are Hampton real estate taxes billed and appealed?

Hampton's city page lists the real estate tax rate at $1.14 per $100 of assessed value. The tax year runs from July 1 to June 30. The Assessor of Real Estate appraises property every year and assesses it at 100 percent of market value.

Bills for the first half are mailed around November 1 and are due December 5. Second-half bills are mailed around May 1 and are due June 5. A 10 percent penalty applies after the due date, and interest of 10 percent a year starts July 1 on unpaid balances. Confirm the current rate with the Hampton real estate tax page before you budget.

An owner who disagrees with an assessment has three steps, described on the city's appeal page:

  • Office Review: file within 30 days of the assessment notice.
  • Board of Review: file within 60 days of the notice. An office review is not required first.
  • Circuit Court: a petition can be filed without using either earlier step.

The assessor's office is at One Franklin Street, Suite 602, and the phone number is 757-727-8311. Hours are Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

What do Hampton sellers usually face?

Hampton sellers often fall into one of a few situations. Each one changes which sale route makes sense.

  • An inherited house in Phoebus, Fox Hill or Wythe that nobody wants to maintain.
  • A military transfer with a fixed report date.
  • Deferred repairs on an older frame house, especially roof, drainage and moisture.
  • A rental with tenants in place.
  • Unpaid taxes or a mortgage that has fallen behind.

A traditional listing can bring a higher price when the house is in good shape and there is time. It also means showings, inspection requests and a buyer's financing contingency. A cash sale trades some of that price for speed and certainty. The right choice depends on the condition of the house and the date you need to close.

If you are weighing a Hampton cash offer, ask for the terms in writing, ask who pays for title work, and compare the net amount you would receive against a listing after repairs, commission and carrying costs.

How does a cash sale of a Hampton house work step by step?

A cash sale skips the buyer's lender, so the timeline depends mostly on the title work. The usual order is a short conversation about the house, a walk-through or photos, a written offer, and then a closing with a title or settlement company.

Before closing, the title company searches the property for liens, unpaid taxes and anything recorded against the owner. In Hampton, that includes any real estate tax installments that are due December 5 or June 5. If the owner has died, the title company will want to see who has authority to sell. Gathering those papers early shortens the process.

You choose the closing date within what the title work allows. You are never obligated to accept an offer.

Hampton covers 136.27 square miles, of which 51.46 are land and the rest is water. The 2020 census counted 137,148 residents, and the Census Bureau estimated 137,315 in 2025.

Does Hampton have a county government?

No. Hampton is an independent city, so the city handles assessment, tax billing and most local services without a county. Hampton merged with Elizabeth City County and the town of Phoebus on July 1, 1952.

When are Hampton real estate taxes due?

The first half is due December 5 and the second half is due June 5, based on the city's tax page. A 10 percent penalty applies to late payments.

How long do I have to appeal my Hampton assessment?

You have 30 days from the assessment notice to request an office review and 60 days to apply to the Board of Review. A Circuit Court petition does not require either earlier step.

Can I sell a Hampton house that needs repairs?

Yes. Many Hampton houses are older and need work, and an as-is cash sale means you do not repair anything before closing. The offer reflects the condition of the house.

Where is Blacksburg, VA, and what kind of town is it?

Blacksburg is an incorporated town in Montgomery County, in the New River Valley of southwest Virginia, at about 2,080 feet above sea level. It is the largest town in the state by population, with 44,826 residents in the 2020 census, and it sits on the Eastern Continental Divide.

The town is part of the Blacksburg-Christiansburg metropolitan area, which also includes Christiansburg, the city of Radford and all of Montgomery, Pulaski and Giles counties. Blacksburg is about 10 miles north of Christiansburg and the I-81 interchange, and the drive to Roanoke by way of US 460 and I-81 usually takes less than an hour.

William Black laid out a 16-block grid in 1797, and the General Assembly established the town on January 13, 1798. The town was incorporated in 1871, and Virginia Agricultural and Mechanical College, now Virginia Tech, opened on October 2, 1872.

Growth stayed modest for most of the next century. The population was 3,358 in 1950 and 9,384 in 1970. Then the 1970s annexed Virginia Tech into the town, and the count jumped to 30,638 by 1980. US 460 is the main road in and out, a four-lane highway linking I-81 at Christiansburg with I-77 in Princeton, West Virginia. The Huckleberry Trail, built on the old railbed, runs through town and is a selling point for houses nearby.

The city annexed South Salem in 1953 and an eastern tract in 1960, so much of the housing was built in stages across the twentieth century. Houses from different decades can carry very different repair needs, from older wiring and plumbing to newer roofs that still need work.

Who lives in Salem, and what does that mean for a sale?

In 2020, 21.0% of Salem residents were aged 65 or over. Nearly a third of households are one person living alone.

That pattern produces a steady flow of houses where an owner has died, moved to assisted living or moved in with family. Heirs often live in another state and have no wish to manage repairs, a vacant house and a probate calendar from a distance.

If that describes your situation, a direct cash sale can shorten the path, because the buyer takes the house in its current condition and the closing date is something you can discuss with the buyer.

What are the main roads and landmarks in Salem?

Salem is crossed by the old Great Road corridor, now US 11, and by Interstate 81. Interstate 81 is the high-speed route past the city.

  • Roanoke College, in central Salem, was chartered in 1853 after the Virginia Institute moved from Staunton in 1847.
  • The Salem RidgeYaks, a Single-A Boston Red Sox affiliate, play in the city.
  • Salem Football Stadium hosted the NCAA Division III championship game, the Stagg Bowl, from 1993 to 2016.
  • The Salem Civic Center and the James I. Moyer Sports Complex have hosted other NCAA events.

Streets near the college and the civic venues tend to see more traffic and event parking. Sellers in those pockets should expect buyers to ask about it.

How do Salem's schools and local government work?

Salem runs its own public school system with four elementary schools: G. W. Carver, South Salem, East Salem and West Salem. Andrew Lewis Middle School and Salem High School serve the older grades.

The city uses a council-manager form of government, with a five-member council that elects a mayor and vice mayor from among its members. A city manager runs day-to-day operations.

For a seller, this keeps things simple. Questions about permits, code complaints, utility accounts and tax bills go to Salem's own departments rather than to Roanoke County.

What taxes and fees apply when you sell a house in Salem?

Virginia charges two deed taxes on a sale, and both are set in the Code of Virginia. The state recordation tax is 25 cents per $100 of the sale price or assessed value, whichever is greater, under section 58.1-801.

The grantor's tax in section 58.1-802 is 50 cents per $500 of value above $100. The seller normally pays it, though the buyer and seller may agree that the buyer covers some or all of it. The deed must state the price on its first page before the clerk will record it.

  • Ask the Salem Treasurer and Commissioner of the Revenue for the current real estate tax due dates and your payoff figure, since we could not confirm them from an official Salem page.
  • Ask the title company to prorate city taxes at closing.
  • Check the clerk of the circuit court that records Salem deeds for current recording charges.

Does an inherited house in Salem have different rules?

Yes, in one respect: Virginia's Residential Property Disclosure Act excludes transfers by a fiduciary who is administering a decedent's estate, a guardianship, a conservatorship or a trust. The list of exclusions in section 55.1-702 also covers transfers between spouses or to lineal relatives, and transfers after a foreclosure sale.

That does not remove your duty to deal honestly with a buyer. It does mean the standard seller disclosure form may not apply to an executor's sale. Ask the estate's attorney which rules cover your transfer before you sign.

How does a cash sale compare with listing a Salem house?

A traditional listing in Salem means preparing the house, showing it, negotiating repairs after an inspection and waiting for a buyer's lender. A cash sale to an investor skips the lender step and usually the repair negotiation.

  • Listing suits houses in good shape where you can wait for the best price.
  • Selling by owner saves an agent's commission but puts marketing and paperwork on you.
  • A cash offer suits inherited, tenant-occupied, damaged or behind-on-payments houses where speed and certainty matter more than top dollar.

Whatever route you choose, compare the net amount you would actually receive, after taxes, repairs and holding costs, rather than the headline number.

More questions about Salem, VA

Is Salem, Virginia part of Roanoke County?

No. Salem is an independent city and a separate jurisdiction, even though it is the county seat of Roanoke County. Salem has its own courthouse and sheriff's office, while the county's administrative offices are in Cave Spring.

Who pays the deed taxes when a house sells in Salem?

The seller normally pays the grantor's tax of 50 cents per $500, and the state recordation tax of 25 cents per $100 is charged on the deed. The buyer and seller can agree to split or shift the grantor's tax. Your closing statement will show the exact amounts.

Can I sell an inherited house in Salem without a listing?

Yes, as long as the person signing has legal authority to sell, such as an executor or a named heir after the estate is settled. Confirm with the estate's attorney before you accept any offer.

How fast can a cash sale close in Salem?

Timing depends on title work, any liens, probate status and when you want to move. A cash buyer does not wait on a mortgage underwriter, so the closing date is often set by the title search rather than financing.

Where is Herndon, VA, and is it a town or a city?

Herndon is an incorporated town in Fairfax County, in Northern Virginia and the Washington, D.C. metro area. It covers 4.29 square miles at an elevation of about 361 feet, and the 2020 census counted 24,655 residents, according to Wikipedia. It is the largest of the three incorporated towns in the county.

A town in Virginia sits inside a county, so Herndon owners deal with two governments. The town runs its own council and its own police department, while Fairfax County handles assessment and tax billing. A little over two acres of the town technically lie in Loudoun County.

How did Herndon develop?

The settlement took the name Herndon in 1858, after naval officer William Lewis Herndon, who died with his ship, the SS Central America, while helping save more than 150 passengers and crew. Many Northern soldiers and families settled here in the 1870s, drawn by the climate and low land prices.

The area grew as a dairy and vacation hub along the Alexandria, Loudoun and Hampshire Railroad, later the Washington and Old Dominion Railroad. The old line is now the W&OD hike and bike trail, and the train station has become the Herndon Depot Museum. The Herndon Historic District is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

Population growth came late. Herndon had 1,960 people in 1960 and 11,449 in 1980, then reached 24,655 in 2020. Most of the town's growth came after 1960, so many houses are from the later twentieth century, with older ones near the historic downtown.

Who are the largest employers in Herndon?

Herndon is part of the Dulles Technology Corridor, and its largest employers are technology and government contractors. Wikipedia reports the principal employers from the town's 2025 Annual Comprehensive Financial Report:

  • Serco: 500 to 749 employees
  • Amazon Web Services, Karsun Solutions, Northwest Federal Credit Union, Peraton and Boeing: 250 to 499 each
  • Town of Herndon, Smartronix, Everfox Holdings and Allwyn: 100 to 249 each

The 2022 American Community Survey figures cited on the same page put median household income in the town at $133,403, and 52.5 percent of residents held a bachelor's degree or higher. Wikipedia also notes that 53.7 percent of residents spoke a language other than English at home.

For a seller, the practical effect is a buyer pool that includes contractors and government workers who can be sensitive to a job change or a security clearance timeline. Those sellers may need to close fast when a relocation arrives.

How do roads and the Metro affect a Herndon address?

State Route 228 runs through the center of town along Elden Street, Monroe Street, Park Avenue and Dranesville Road. A truck route follows Herndon Parkway around downtown. At the south end of town, Route 228 meets State Route 267, the Dulles Toll Road, which leads to Washington via Interstate 66 and to Dulles International Airport.

The Silver Line extension opened in 2022 with service at Herndon station. A house within walking or short driving distance of the station can attract a different set of buyers than one on a cul-de-sac away from it, though the effect on any single sale varies.

Within the town, every residence is within a mile of a public park, and the town has a community center, an aquatic center and the Herndon Centennial Golf Course.

Who lives in Herndon, and what does that say about the housing?

The median age in Herndon was 35.1 in the 2020 census. About 24.8 percent of residents were under 18 and 10.0 percent were 65 or older. Of the 7,900 households, 39.6 percent included children, and 53.6 percent were married-couple households.

The town had 8,133 housing units in 2020, with a homeowner vacancy rate of 0.6 percent and a rental vacancy rate of 4.0 percent. Few homes in the town were sitting empty, which says nothing about the price of any one house.

The town also hosts regular events, including the Friday Night Live concerts from May to August, a farmers market from May to October and a Labor Day jazz festival, which add to the appeal of the downtown blocks near the depot.

Which schools serve Herndon?

Herndon belongs to the Fairfax County Public Schools district. The public schools that serve students inside the town limits are Clearview, Dranesville, Herndon and Hutchison elementary schools, Herndon Middle School and Herndon High School.

Private options include Dominion Christian School and St. Joseph's Elementary, along with several Montessori schools. Nearby in Floris are King Abdullah Academy and the Nysmith School. Zoning to a particular school can change, so confirm attendance boundaries with the district for a specific address.

How are Herndon real estate taxes billed?

Herndon's town tax is collected by Fairfax County and shows up on the Fairfax County real estate bill. The town's page lists a Fiscal Year 2027 rate of $0.27 per $100 of assessed value. The county sets its own rate separately, so check the county's tax pages for the full bill.

The due dates are July 28 for the first installment and December 5 for the second. Late balances carry additional penalties and interest. The Fairfax County Department of Tax Administration answers assessment and payment questions at (703) 222-8234 or DTARED@fairfaxcounty.gov, and it also runs the tax relief program. See the Town of Herndon real estate tax page for details.

Because two installments land in July and December, a closing near either date should account for who pays the bill that is due. Your title company can prorate it.

What do Herndon sellers commonly face?

Sellers in a high-cost commuter town often face the same handful of issues.

  • An owner who bought years ago and now lives out of the area, with a house that needs updating.
  • An inherited house shared among several heirs who disagree on timing.
  • A rental that has been through several tenants.
  • Deferred repairs that make a bank appraisal or buyer inspection risky.

Rules specific to historic properties, permits and rentals are set by the town and the county. We could not open those Herndon pages, so contact the town's community development staff before you plan work or a rental.

How does a cash sale work in Herndon?

A cash sale means the buyer does not need a mortgage. You describe the house, receive a written offer and, if you accept, the title or settlement company handles liens, tax proration and recording. Closing can be arranged around your date.

An as-is sale is often the simplest way out of a house that would need major work. Compare it with the cost of repairs, agent fees and months of mortgage, tax and utility payments on a listing. The net figure matters more than the headline price.
